questions.question: How do you keep track of the money you spend each month?
questions.model_answer: I write my spending in a notes app once a day. At the end of the month, I sort those notes into food, transport, and other bills.

questions.question: What is one expense you watch carefully, and why?
questions.model_answer: I watch food spending most carefully, because small snacks add up before I notice them. Packing lunch is how I keep that weekly amount steady.

questions.set_intro: Imagine that a magazine writer is collecting stories about daily life in your country. You agreed to answer a few questions by phone about household budgets.
questions.question: Would you recommend that someone in a first job write a monthly budget? Why or why not?
questions.model_answer: Yes, I would recommend a written monthly budget to someone in a first job. A new salary can disappear on rent and meals before the person notices. A simple page with income at the top and three spending groups is enough to start. It also shows whether there is room to save a small amount. That habit is easier to build in the first month than after a year.

questions.question: Should employers give workers one paid day each year to volunteer in the community? Say whether you agree, and support your view with reasons and an example.
questions.model_answer: I agree that employers should give workers one paid day each year to volunteer in the community. A paid day makes service possible for people who cannot afford to lose a day's wages, so the help does not fall only on those with spare money. It can also build real ties between a company and the town around it. For example, a staff team could spend the day planting trees in a schoolyard or sorting food at a neighborhood pantry. They would then understand local needs better than they would from a poster. The day should be optional and arranged with a trusted local group, but offering it is still a practical and fair way to support the wider community.
